clue.text: Figure, by the sound of it, taken already

indicators.note: says the phrase heard aloud gives letters spelt differently

parts.note: a figure such as four, when it is spoken, is a 'spoken four'

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a figure and is told, apparently, that it has already been claimed.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the number four out loud and you have a 'spoken four', which is heard exactly like the phrase for something already reserved.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spoken for has been reserved or claimed, so it is no longer available.

clue.text: Pilot, one looking round back of cockpit

indicators.note: one looking round something holds it inside, so the seer goes around the next letter

parts.note: with 'looking' the clue reads 'one looking', but only 'one' is the leaf here: a SEER is one who sees

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

parts.note: its last letter is T

explanation.surface: A pilot glances over a shoulder towards the rear of the cockpit.
explanation.walkthrough: SEER (one who looks) goes round T, the last letter of 'cockpit'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pilot a vessel is to steer it, guiding its course.

clue.text: Month, eg October, not entirely busy

indicators.note: says only part of the words is used, the answer sitting inside them

parts.note: the letters run from inside 'Month' through 'eg' into 'October'

explanation.surface: October is described as a month that is never entirely busy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the go is constantly active, the idiom for being busy.

clue.text: Icon in document allowing entry to Spain, briefly?

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its last letter

parts.note: a visa allows entry; in Spain, mock-Spanish style, it is 'el visa'
the last letter dropped

explanation.surface: An icon appears inside the paperwork a traveller needs to enter Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: dressing 'visa' with the Spanish article 'el' makes ELVISA, and dropping the final letter leaves the singer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley is a cultural icon, one of the most recognised figures in popular music.

clue.text: Writer experienced upset

parts.note: to have felt something is to have experienced it
to tip something is to upset or overturn it

explanation.surface: An author is said to have experienced being upset.
explanation.definitionFit: A felt-tip is a pen, an implement one writes with.

clue.text: Sovereign taken from lender, price after adjustment correct

indicators.note: says the sovereign's letters are removed from the words that follow
the remaining letters are rearranged, adjusted into a new order

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword monarch

explanation.surface: A monarch borrows from a lender, and the price is put right after a negotiation.
explanation.walkthrough: Pool the letters of LENDER and PRICE, take out E and R (ER, the Queen), and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: To red-pencil a text is to mark errors in it, as an editor or teacher would.

clue.text: See 13
Trouble after groups go to sea

indicators.note: says the trouble comes after the groups

parts.note: sets are groups
to ail is to trouble, as an illness does

explanation.surface: Trouble breaks out after a band of people head off on a voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: To set sail is to begin a sea voyage.

clue.text: Players beginning in harmony in interpretation of score: music, say, arising?

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is placed inside it
an interpretation of the letters gives them a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is H

indicators.note: in a down clue, arising means reading upwards, so backwards

parts.note: music is an example of art

explanation.surface: Musicians start playing in harmony as they interpret a score, music rising up.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of 'harmony' goes into ORCES, a rearrangement of SCORE; then ART (music being an example), read upwards as TRA, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large group of musicians, the players of an ensemble.

clue.text: See 14
Separate cape rounded by unpopular revolutionary

indicators.note: says the cape is surrounded by the other letters
a revolution turns something round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: someone unpopular is hated
C is the map abbreviation for cape

explanation.surface: A disliked rebel surrounds a headland, splitting it off.
explanation.definitionFit: To separate one thing from another is to detach it.

clue.text: See 16
Generate slops for grunter living in pigsty?

indicators.note: to slop is to slosh about messily, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Feeding a pig: producing slops for a grunting animal in its sty.
explanation.walkthrough: The grunter in a pigsty looks like a pig, but it is the stereotypical adolescent who grunts replies and lives in a messy bedroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolescents are joked about as monosyllabic grunters whose untidy rooms resemble a pigsty.

clue.text: Blank charter on Gibraltar not entirely backed

indicators.note: backed means read in reverse, back to front
says only part of the words is used

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'charter' through 'on' into 'Gibraltar'

explanation.surface: A charter about Gibraltar is left incomplete and lacks support.
explanation.definitionFit: To blank someone is to snub them, deliberately paying them no attention.

clue.text: Serious rubbish sadly, or time when few watch?

parts.note: grave means serious

indicators.note: rubbish suggests something messed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Solemn junk, sadly, or perhaps a dead hour on the schedule?
explanation.walkthrough: GRAVE for serious, then the letters of SADLY OR plus T for time are scrambled, 'rubbish' as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A graveyard slot is a broadcasting period, late at night, with very small audiences.

clue.text: Comically delivers a bunfight and something edgy — does this?

definitions.text: Comically delivers a bunfight and something edgy — does this?

indicators.note: something done comically is done in a madcap way, so these letters are thrown about

parts.note: anagram fodder
a fringe is an edge, something at the edge

explanation.surface: A comedy show delivers knockabout and edginess: that is what this event does.
explanation.walkthrough: The seventeen letters of DELIVERS A BUNFIGHT rearrange to the Scottish capital's festival; FRINGE (an edge) completes it, and the whole clue describes the event's comic, edgy shows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is the vast August arts festival famous for comedy and experimental shows.

clue.text: Nick, Paul etc wasted energy

indicators.note: wasted means wrecked, so the letters are ruined into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder; Paul is the setter's own name
anagram fodder
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Nick and the setter Paul, and the rest, have squandered their energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name alongside Paul, but it is the verb meaning steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To peculate is to embezzle, and to nick is British slang for to steal.

clue.text: Those such as eyes left in the sack?

definitions.text: Those such as eyes left in the sack?

parts.words: Those such as eyes left in the sack?
parts.note: 'Eyes left' is a parade-ground command, one of a type of military instruction, and the same phrase also means a dismissal, getting the sack

explanation.walkthrough: 'Eyes left' suggests someone's eyes lying in a bag, but it is a drill command; the plural phrase for such commands is also slang for being fired.
explanation.definitionFit: Marching orders are commands to troops on the move, and figuratively notice of dismissal from a job.

clue.text: Something attractive: verse for just three of six wives?

parts.note: three of Henry VIII's six wives were called Catherine, shortened to CATH
an ode is a poem, a piece of verse

explanation.surface: A poem written for only half of a king's six wives, the alluring ones.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry VIII had six wives, three of them named Catherine: an ODE for a CATH.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathode is an electrode that attracts positively charged ions in electrolysis.

clue.text: Relation, though not well-spoken, accepted linguistic rules

indicators.note: says the word is as said in a sloppy, non-standard accent, where the D is dropped

parts.note: a grandma is a relation

explanation.surface: A relative who speaks poorly nonetheless accepted the rules of language.
explanation.walkthrough: In careless speech 'grandma' comes out as 'gramma', which in a non-rhotic British accent sounds like the word for language rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar is the set of rules governing how words are combined in a language.

clue.text: Reportedly, wood supporter behind very rotten tree, back part

indicators.note: says the supporter comes after the rest
says the word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: lumber is cut timber, wood

indicators.note: rotten suggests decay, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
a bra is a supporting garment

explanation.surface: Wood propping up a decaying tree, behind which something gives support to the back.
explanation.walkthrough: LUMBAR is heard as LUMBER (wood); then V for very and ERTE (a rearrangement of TREE, 'rotten'), with BRA (supporter) behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A lumbar vertebra is one of the bones of the lower spine, part of the back.

clue.text: Jersey's post collection

parts.note: mail is post
a lot is a collection, as at auction

explanation.surface: The Channel Island of Jersey's postal collection.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey looks like the island, but it is a garment: the French-derived name for a cycling or dancer's jersey.
explanation.definitionFit: A maillot is a close-fitting top, as in the yellow maillot of the Tour de France.

clue.text: See 19
See 14
See 24
Person imprisoned by king, hopeless case

indicators.note: says the person is held inside the king's letters

parts.note: GR, Georgius Rex, is the abbreviation for King George
one is a person, as in 'one never knows'

explanation.surface: A man locked up by the monarch is a lost cause.
explanation.definitionFit: A goner is someone beyond help, doomed or certain to fail.

clue.text: Working body in Dog and Duck caught in drunken furore

parts.note: a lab is a Labrador
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is placed inside it
drunken means staggering about, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A rowdy scene at the Dog and Duck pub, where someone is caught up in a drunken uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: Dog and Duck reads as a pub name, but gives LAB and O; then C (caught) goes inside URFORE, a rearrangement of FURORE.
explanation.definitionFit: The labour force is a nation's working population, those employed or available for employment.

clue.text: Streaky appearance put stain on flashy stuff

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or put a stain on
bling is showy jewellery, flashy stuff

explanation.surface: Someone spills on gaudy jewellery, leaving it looking streaked.
explanation.definitionFit: Marbling is a veined, mottled pattern that imitates the streaks in marble.

clue.text: Do little swivel, diver partially turns

indicators.note: turns says the hidden letters are read backwards
partially says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A diver does little more than swivel and turn in the water.
explanation.definitionFit: To idle is to laze, being inactive and accomplishing little.

clue.text: Machine possibly combined with server that almost crashed

indicators.note: something crashed is wrecked, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the word, the final letter dropped

parts.note: almost all of that, losing its last letter
the dropped letter

explanation.surface: A computer server that very nearly crashed is mixed up with some machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Combined' hints at the full name: a combine harvester. The letters of SERVER plus THA (most of 'that') are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A harvester is a farm machine for gathering crops, often joined to a thresher as a combine harvester.
